steps.body: A whole can be traded for denominator-sized pieces without changing the amount. The model writes 2 1/4 as 9/4; similarly, 4 1/8 can be regrouped as 3 9/8.
steps.narration: A whole can be traded for denominator-sized pieces without changing the amount. The model writes 2 1/4 as 9/4; similarly, 4 1/8 can be regrouped as 3 9/8.

widget.prompt: After trading one whole, 4 1/8 has how many eighths in its fraction part? Build it.
widget.successFeedback: 9/8 — the original one eighth plus the eight that came from the traded whole.
widget.lowFeedback: That build is SHORTER than 9/8 — either shade more pieces or make each piece larger until the lengths match.
widget.highFeedback: That build is LONGER than 9/8 — either shade fewer pieces or make each piece smaller until the lengths match.

commonFractions.feedback: 1/8 is the fraction part BEFORE the trade; a whole has yet to be broken.
8/8 is the traded whole alone; the eighth already there joins it.

predict.reveal: Flipping answers a different question; trading makes the real subtraction possible.

cml.actionGoal: Rename both fractions to the same piece size, then count the pieces for g5u regroup.
invariants: Fractions add and subtract only when their pieces are the same size: renaming scales both parts of a fraction and leaves its value untouched, which is what makes g5u regroup a counting problem once the denominators agree.
misconceptions: Adding numerators and denominators across, scaling only one part of a fraction when renaming, or forgetting to trade a whole when the top fraction is too small to subtract from.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If only the numerators were made equal instead of the denominators, what would go wrong?

widget.prompt: Subtracting 4 1/8 − 1 5/8, the fraction parts give 1/8 − 5/8. What is the legal move?

options.label: Trade one whole from the 4 for 8/8, making it 3 9/8
options.feedback: Correct — one whole is eight eighths, so 9/8 − 5/8 = 4/8 and the wholes become 3 − 1.

options.label: Compute 5/8 − 1/8 instead
options.feedback: Flipping the subtraction answers a different question, exactly as it would with whole numbers.

options.label: Say the answer has no fraction part
options.feedback: There is a fraction part; it just needs a trade before it can be found.

options.label: Add the fractions instead
options.feedback: The problem subtracts. Trading makes the subtraction possible without changing it.

hints: Trade when the top is short.
